approach: Root cause: the baseline records only whether a whole check failed on the base. `Baseline::failed_before` matches by check name, and `verify::is_pre_existing` uses it, so a check that failed on the base excuses every failure inside it. That includes a new, different test failure and a failure from a clash with a concurrent change. Fix it at that comparison. Add `failed_tests: Vec<String>` (serde default, skipped when empty) to `CheckRun`. Add a parser in `checks.rs` that reads the `failures:` list from cargo test output, qualified by test binary. `run_check` fills the field for test-kind checks from the full output before the tail is cut. `baseline_runs` calls `run_check`, so the baseline and the candidate runs share one field and one parser. `Baseline::failed_tests_before` returns the base's names. `is_pre_existing` becomes per test: when both sides have names, the check is pre-existing only if every failing test also failed on the base. When either side has none (fmt, clippy, build errors, timeouts, old records), it keeps the name-level rule. `judge` adds a finding for a blocking check with names, splitting newly failing tests from tests already failing on the base. No governance file changes. The one-line `failed_tests: Vec::new()` additions in files outside the deliverable list are forced by the compiler, because Rust struct literals must name every field. They carry no logic, and a missed one breaks `cargo clippy --all-targets`. Each is listed in `files` for that reason.

decisions.choice: Record failing test names on `CheckRun` (new optional field), so the baseline and the candidate run share one shape and one parser.
decisions.reason: The origin is that the baseline holds a pass/fail bit per check. `run_check` produces both the baseline runs (via `baseline_runs`) and the candidate runs, so one field filled there fixes both sides. `output_tail` cannot serve: it is capped at 4 KiB and keeps only the tail.

rejected.why: The tail is cut to the last 4096 bytes, so a long failure list would be truncated and a failing test could be missed.

rejected.option: Add the names only to `Baseline` and keep `CheckRun` unchanged, to avoid editing about ten literal sites outside the deliverables
rejected.why: The candidate side needs names too, and the candidate runs travel as `Vec<CheckRun>` through run/mod.rs, `mark_pre_existing`, `held_for_timeout` and `judge`. Carrying them separately would change every one of those signatures. That is a larger change than the mechanical literal additions.

rejected.option: Hide the names in the existing `note` or `output_tail` text
rejected.why: It overloads fields that other code reads as prose, for example `timed_out` matches on the note, and it avoids the compile-forced edits only by making a hidden format.

decisions.choice: Fall back to the name-level rule whenever either side has no parsed names. When both have names, a candidate whose names are all in the base's names is pre-existing; any other name is new.
decisions.reason: It keeps fmt and clippy, build errors, timeouts and records written before the change behaving as today, and it tightens only the case where per-test evidence exists on both sides.

rejected.option: Treat a candidate failure without names as new when the base had names
rejected.why: It changes timeout and held-for-timeout behaviour (`held_for_timeout` calls `is_pre_existing`), which is beyond one focused change. Recorded as an open question.

decisions.choice: Qualify each name with its test binary (taken from the `Running ...` or `Doc-tests ...` line, hash suffix stripped).
decisions.reason: The same test name can exist in several crates. An unqualified match could excuse a new failure that shares a name with a base failure.

decisions.choice: Report the split as an Athena finding from `judge`, naming new and already-failing tests, and leave the existing `check X failed` reasons unchanged.
decisions.reason: Tests assert the `check test failed` reason text, and the finding is what the user reads in a rejected job. A partial overlap is not pre-existing, so `mark_pre_existing` does not mark it. A check with no names produces no finding, so existing behaviour is unchanged.

rejected.why: The note is not shown where the verdict is explained, and a partially overlapping check is not marked pre-existing.

risks.risk: `CheckRun` has `deny_unknown_fields`, so records written by the new code with names would not parse on an older binary.
risks.mitigation: Use `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]`. Records without names serialise as before. The old-record parse test and the existing round-trip tests cover it.

risks.risk: About 20 `CheckRun` literals across the files above must gain the field, and a missed one breaks the build.
risks.mitigation: The compiler lists every missed literal. The file list came from grepping `CheckRun {` across crates, and `cargo clippy --all-targets` compiles the tests.

risks.risk: The `failures:` format varies: the first `failures:` block holds stdout sections, and doc-tests and several binaries each print their own list.
risks.mitigation: Qualify names with the binary from the `Running`/`Doc-tests` line. Read only the `failures:` list lines (4-space indent) up to the first blank line. Test on real output shapes quoted in the two jobs.

risks.risk: A flaky test that fails on both base and candidate is excused, and a differently named flaky test now blocks.
risks.mitigation: With names on both sides this is the intended tightening, and the tests pin both directions. The fallback applies only when a side has no names.

risks.risk: The new finding adds a Major finding next to the existing `check test failed` reason and could double-count in send-back.
risks.mitigation: The reasons and verdict logic are otherwise unchanged. Run the send_back tests (`run/send_back.rs` calls `judge`), and fall to Minor if they count it twice.

risks.risk: Brief rules ask for a refusal-corpus mapping when a parser is added.
risks.mitigation: Not applicable: the change adds no refusal or matching rule over requests or readings, so the refusal corpus is not touched. I did not read `refusal_corpus.rs` and cite no case ids. The test-name parser has its own unit tests.

demonstrations.method: Unit tests in the verify.rs tests module build a baseline with the existing `baseline_with` and candidate `CheckRun`s whose `failed_tests` is set. They call `is_pre_existing`, `mark_pre_existing` and `judge` through the existing `judge_against`. Cases: base {X} against candidate {X,Y} is not pre-existing, the verdict is Fail, and a finding names Y. Base {X} against candidate {X} is pre-existing and passes with no reasons. Base {X} against candidate {Y} is not pre-existing.
demonstrations.observes: The tests pass, including the assertion that Y is named and the companion case where only X fails stays pre-existing.
demonstrations.fails_without: Without the per-test comparison, `is_pre_existing` matches by check name, so base {X} against candidate {X,Y} is marked pre-existing and the verdict passes. The assertions that the check is not pre-existing, the verdict is Fail and Y is named would fail.
demonstrations.seam: Production entry points `verify::is_pre_existing`, `mark_pre_existing` and `judge` (exist; verify.rs around lines 134-151 and 282). Fixtures are the existing helpers `baseline_with`, `judge_against` and `check` in the verify.rs tests (they exist). Step 3 makes `check` carry an empty `failed_tests` list and the tests set it directly on real records. There is no fake, and the comparison logic is not in any double.

demonstrations.method: Unit tests in checks.rs call `failed_test_names(&str)` with literal cargo output. One multi-binary run has two failing tests under `failures:` and `Running unittests ...` lines, so names come out qualified by binary. One doc-test failure. One output with only a `---- name stdout ----` block and no list. One output with no failures. A `run_check` test uses `sh -c printf ...` for a `CheckKind::Test` spec and checks that `CheckRun.failed_tests` is filled. A verify.rs test checks that a check without names falls back to the name-level rule (base fails and candidate fails is pre-existing).
demonstrations.observes: Names are extracted. Output with no list gives an empty result. The empty result leads to the name-level rule.
demonstrations.fails_without: Without the parser, `failed_test_names` does not exist and the extraction and `run_check` tests cannot pass. A wrong parser, for example one that reads the first `failures:` stdout section or the `test ... FAILED` lines, would give wrong names and fail the exact-name assertions.
demonstrations.seam: Production entry points `checks::failed_test_names` (added in step 2), `checks::run_check` (exists, checks.rs line 190) and `verify::is_pre_existing` (exists). Fixture: a `sh_spec`-style spec (the helper exists in the checks.rs tests; the new test sets `kind` to Test) that prints the cargo output with `printf`, injected as the `CheckSpec` argument to `run_check`. The output is canned text and the parsing runs in production code.

It parses that through `AnyRecord::parse` and `check_record_file` at `baseline.json`, then calls `Baseline::validate`. demonstrations.fails_without: If `failed_tests` lacked `#[serde(default)]`, old JSON would fail to parse under `deny_unknown_fields` and `check_record_file`. If it lacked `skip_serializing_if`, existing serialised records would change shape and the round-trip and old-shape tests would fail.

demonstrations.method: A verify.rs test judges base {X} against candidate {X,Y} through the existing `judge_against` and reads the Athena finding. It asserts the evidence lists Y under newly failing and X under already failing on the base. A second case with only new names has no 'already' part. A third case, a check with no names, yields no such finding.

demonstrations.fails_without: Without the finding, `judge` returns only the `check test failed` reason and no text that separates the tests, so the assertions on the finding's summary and evidence would fail.

open_questions: When the base failed with test names and the candidate check fails with none (build error or timeout), the plan keeps the name-level rule, which still excuses it. A stricter rule would change `held_for_timeout`, so it is left out of this change.

Should the finding be Major, as planned, or Minor? Major adds to the blocker/major count, but the check already fails the verdict. The producer should confirm against `send_back` behaviour when running the tests.
